why: pandas is how analysts and data engineers explore and clean data in Python. Take-home tests are very often a pandas notebook.
outcome: load a messy file, clean it, aggregate it and export a result you can trust.

lessons.title: Load and inspect a DataFrame
text: A DataFrame is a table: columns have names and types, rows have an index. Start every analysis by looking at the shape, the types and a few rows.
read_csv, read_excel and read_parquet cover most inputs. Parse dates when loading so you can filter by time later.
points: df["col"] is one column (a Series); df[["a", "b"]] is a smaller DataFrame.
df.loc[rows, cols] selects by labels; df.iloc[...] by position.
Filter rows with a boolean mask: df[df["salary"] > 40000].

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("jobs.csv", parse_dates=["posted_at"])
print(df.shape)
print(df.dtypes)
paris = df[(df["city"] == "Paris") & (df["salary"] >= 45000)]
print(paris[["title", "company", "salary"]].head())

lessons.title: Clean: missing values, types, duplicates
text: Real data has missing values, numbers stored as text, extra spaces and duplicates. Clean in small, explicit steps you can explain.
Decide per column what a missing value means: drop the row, fill a default, or keep it as unknown.
points: df.isna().sum() counts missing values per column.
df["salary"] = pd.to_numeric(df["salary"], errors="coerce") turns bad text into NaN.
Chain steps with .assign() to keep the original data untouched.

example.code:
clean = (
    df.drop_duplicates(subset=["title", "company"])
      .assign(
          city=lambda d: d["city"].str.strip().str.title(),
          salary=lambda d: pd.to_numeric(d["salary"], errors="coerce"),
      )
      .dropna(subset=["title"])
)
print(clean.isna().sum())

lessons.title: Aggregate, join and reshape
text: groupby + agg answers most business questions: per city, per month, per category. merge joins two DataFrames like a SQL JOIN.
pivot_table turns rows into columns for a report-style view.
points: pd.merge(a, b, on="company_id", how="left") keeps every row of a.
Check row counts after a merge, as in SQL.
df.to_csv("out.csv", index=False) or df.to_excel(...) to share.

items: Text to number, bad values to NaN

pitfalls: Modifying a filtered slice and getting SettingWithCopyWarning: use .loc or .assign on a copy.
Forgetting parentheses around each condition when combining with & and |.
Averaging a column that still contains text or wrong types.
Losing rows silently in an inner merge.

exercises.q: Return the 3 companies with the most offers in the DataFrame df.

df.pivot_table(index="month", columns="city", values="title", aggfunc="count", fill_value=0)

interview.q: How do you deal with missing values?
interview.a: First measure them per column and understand why they are missing. Then choose per column: drop rows if few and random, fill with a meaningful default (0, median, 'unknown') if justified, or keep them and handle them explicitly. Document the choice because it changes the results.
loc selects by labels (index values and column names, end inclusive); iloc selects by integer position like Python slicing (end exclusive).

interview.q: How is merge different from concat?
interview.a: merge joins tables side by side on key columns, like a SQL JOIN. concat stacks tables on top of each other (or side by side by index) without matching keys.
